newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW-Australia heads for 40 MT cane crush.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Australia heads for 40 MT cane crush.

text.p: Australia was headed towards a sugar cane crush of more than 40 million tonnes in 1997 for the first time, Ian Ballantyne, general manager of farmer organisation CANEGROWERS, said on Wednesday.
Cane farmers are is also drawing some optimism from signs of an improvement in the world market, he told Reuters.

With Australia's sugar cane crush underway, the main sugar state of Queensland would certainly crush more than 38 million tonnes of cane this year, up from 37.2 million tonnes in 1996, Ballantyne said in a telephone interview from Brisbane.

Including the minor sugar-producing state of New South Wales (NSW), which had a crop of 2.4 million tonnes in 1996, the total Australian crush in 1997 would be more than 40 million tonnes, Ballantyne said.
"At the moment it would appear to be a sixth successive record (crush), but not by a huge amount," he said. "We expect (the total crush) will be at least 40 (million tonnes)."

Firmer figures would not be available until the crush was further underway, when the impact of March's Cyclone Justin in Queensland's north and the dry period in the south of the state could be more accurately assessed, he said.
Asked whether Queensland's crush of more than 38 million tonnes would yield about 5.1 million tonnes of raw sugar, Ballantyne replied: "How long is a bit of string?"
Justin would have caused a significant reduction of sugar content in cane in Queensland's north, he said.
Last season's crush produced about 5.15 million tonnes of raw sugar but the figure of tonnes of sugar in cane could vary by five percent, he said.
"Certainly a sugar make of around about last year's is expected. The reality is that it could be five percent up and it could be five percent down," he said.
Weather patterns over the next 20 weeks would also have an effect. "We've got an inexact science here," Ballantyne said.

Queensland's sugar crush, which this year began on June 2, has seen 15 or 16 mills start slightly earlier than last year to handle the bigger crop. A late finish would impact on the following season, Ballantyne said.
Price expectations indicated that total returns for the 1997 crop in the ground would be down on last year.
But the market had firmed in the last couple of weeks, backed by expectations that world supply and demand was returning closer to a balance after last year's surplus.
Hopefully this indicated stronger markets for 1998/99, when a supply deficiency was now being predicted, he said.
"We're not being bullish about the future but I think there's a little bit more confidence in the industry now than three or six months ago," Ballantyne said.

The firming market partly reflected a drop in Indian production, from the suplus of more than two million tonnes last year which helped drive prices down, despite an absence of Indian exports, he said.
Indian production was likely to fall by more than three million tonnes this year, he said.
Thailand's crop would be bigger than last year but would also be slightly less than earlier expected, he said.
"There's a little bit more confidence there. We're not expecting any boom price but we would hope we've seen close to the bottom," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
